title: How Deep Does the Ocean Really Go?
description: Drop Mount Everest into the deepest part of the ocean and its summit would still sit more than two kilometers underwater. This is a journey from the surface to the very bottom of the sea — through the zones where sunlight gives out, pressure climbs past a thousand atmospheres, and life stops needing the sun at all.

beats.say: Take the tallest mountain on Earth, Mount Everest, and drop it into the deepest part of the ocean. Its summit would still be more than 2,000 meters underwater.
Twelve people have walked on the Moon. Only a few dozen have ever been to the very bottom of the sea. We know the far side of other worlds better than we know the floor of our own planet.
So today, we're going down. All the way down. Past the reach of sunlight, past the crushing pressure, to a place where life has learned to live without the sun at all.
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, and holds almost all of the planet's water. But from up here, you only ever see the thinnest skin of it.

The top 200 meters is called the sunlight zone. It's where almost everything you picture when you think of the ocean actually lives: the coral reefs, the fish, the sea turtles, and the plankton that make a large share of the oxygen we breathe.

But even here, the light is already disappearing. Water swallows color. Red is gone within the first few meters, then orange, then yellow, until only blue is left. That's why the deep ocean looks blue before it looks black.

Every ten meters you descend, the pressure on your body increases by roughly one whole atmosphere. At the bottom of the sunlight zone, you're already feeling about 20 times the pressure you feel standing on a beach.

Below 200 meters, we enter the twilight zone. It stretches down to 1,000 meters, and here the sunlight is far too weak for plants to grow. There is light, but only barely, a faint blue glow fading into darkness.
And yet this is one of the busiest places on the planet. Every night, countless small animals swim up from the twilight zone to feed near the surface, then sink back down before sunrise.
It's often described as the largest migration on Earth, and it happens every single night, completely out of sight.
Many of the animals making this journey are lanternfish, small fish covered in tiny lights. They may be the most numerous vertebrates on the planet, and yet almost nobody has ever seen one alive.
Down here, being seen is dangerous. So animals have evolved to be transparent, or silver, or bright red, a color that looks black once the red light is gone.
At 1,000 meters, the last trace of sunlight is gone. This is the midnight zone, and from here to the bottom, it is completely dark, forever. The water is cold, just a few degrees above freezing.
But it isn't black. In one major survey of the open ocean, about 76 percent of the animals scientists observed could make their own light. Down here, light is a language.

stat.label: of observed ocean animals can make light

beats.say: Animals flash to find a mate, to lure in prey, or to startle a predator. Some even light up their bellies to erase their own shadow against the faint glow from above.

The anglerfish is the most famous hunter of the dark. A glowing lure dangles in front of its jaws, and anything curious enough to swim toward the light becomes dinner. In some species, the male fuses onto the female's body for the rest of his life.
Sperm whales, the largest predators with teeth on Earth, dive past 2,000 meters to hunt here, holding their breath for over an hour in total darkness.
The Titanic rests in this darkness too, about 3,800 meters down. It took more than seventy years for anyone to find it.
The average depth of the ocean is about 3,700 meters. Below 4,000 meters, we reach the abyss, the vast, flat plains that cover more of our planet than all the continents combined.
Food is scarce here. Almost everything that lives in the abyss depends on a slow drift of dead material falling from far above. Scientists call it marine snow.

Some of that snow takes weeks to reach the bottom. Animals here move slowly, grow slowly, and live a long time. Some deep sea corals are thousands of years old, among the oldest living things on Earth.
When something big does fall, like a whale, it becomes a feast that can feed a whole community of scavengers for years.
And here's the strangest part: we have mapped the surface of Mars in more detail than most of our own seafloor. Only about 25 percent of the ocean floor has been mapped with modern sonar.

stat.label: of the seafloor mapped with modern sonar

beats.say: In 1977, scientists exploring the seafloor near the Galapagos Islands found something no one expected: cracks in the ocean floor pouring out water hotter than 300 degrees Celsius.
The water doesn't boil, because the pressure is so enormous. And around these vents lives an entire ecosystem: giant tube worms up to two meters long, crabs, shrimp and clams.
None of it runs on sunlight. Bacteria here make food from chemicals in the vent water, a process called chemosynthesis, and everything else eats the bacteria.
Some scientists think the very first life on Earth may have started at vents just like these, billions of years ago, long before anything learned to use sunlight.
That discovery changed how we think about life itself. If life can thrive in total darkness, fed by the heat of the planet, it might exist on the ice-covered moons of Jupiter and Saturn too.
Below 6,000 meters are the trenches, deep scars where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The deepest of all is the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, in the western Pacific.
To picture how deep that is: you could stack nearly thirty Empire State Buildings on top of each other and still not reach the surface.
Its floor lies nearly 11,000 meters down. The pressure there is more than 1,000 times what you feel at the surface, like the weight of several cars pressing on every square inch of your body.

In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh sealed themselves into a vessel called the Trieste and sank to the bottom. They stayed for about twenty minutes, and saw almost nothing through the cloud of silt they stirred up.
It was more than fifty years before anyone went back. In 2012, the filmmaker James Cameron made the dive alone.
And even down here, there is life. In 2022, a snailfish was filmed 8,336 meters deep, deeper than any fish had ever been seen before.
Scientists describe new marine species every year, and most of the deep sea has never been seen by a human eye or a camera. The largest habitat on Earth is still mostly unexplored.

So the next time you stand on a beach and look out at the water, remember: you're looking at the surface of a world that goes down eleven kilometers, lit by animals, fed by volcanoes, and still almost entirely unknown.
If you could go down in a submarine to any depth in the ocean, how deep would you go? Tell me in the comments. And if you liked this journey, there's plenty more where it came from.
